extracted.intended_audience: readers and translators of Rabelais; writers, translators of satire, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for translating and prefacing a satirical/lively literary work (Rabelais) so it pleases readers while preserving authorial sense and style. Includes advice on preface tone, audience expectations, and the translator’s proper role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface strategy: bully (railing) vs wheedle (flattery)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two sorts of taking prefaces... Some have bullied many of you into applause, and railed at your faults that you might think them without any; and others, more safely, have spoken kindly of you, that you might think, or at least speak, as favourably of them, and be flattered into patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches have limits: bullying is hard because in this age it's easy to find a bully without courage; flattery pleases when particular but is hated when general. The translator suggests blending the two—'from this marriage of huffing and cringing, there will result a new kind of careless medley'—as a potentially effective, novel strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential qualities of a successful satirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: If uncommon worth, lively wit, and deep learning, wove into wholesome satire, a bold, good, and vast design admirably pursued, truth set out in its true light, and a method how to arrive to its oracle, can recommend a work...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined elements (worth, wit, learning, wholesome satire, bold/design, truth, method) form a substantive standard: a reasonable man will be pleased by a work exhibiting them. Usefulness and entertainment arise from this mixture rather than mere verbosity or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator’s duty: give the author’s sense and copy style where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The first pretence of Mr. Translator... is that of giving his author’s sense in its full extent, and copying his style, if it is to be copied; since he has no share in the invention or disposition of what he translates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate faithfully: convey the author's meaning fully and reproduce his style when called for. The translator should not claim authorship of invention or rearrangement; fidelity to sense and idiom is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation as an act requiring as much genius as invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Some indeed have deservedly gained esteem by translating; yet not many condescend to translate, but such as cannot invent; though to do the first well requires often as much genius as to do the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality translation demands significant creative intelligence—expect difficulty and recognize translation as a craft of near-equal artistic value to original composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty due to linguistic and cultural differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The obsolete words and turns of phrase, and dark subjects, often as darkly treated, make the sense hard to be understood even by a Frenchman, and it cannot be easy to give it the free easy air of an original; for even what seems most common talk in one language, is what is often the most difficult to be made so in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for obsolete terms, culturally specific turns, and dense/dark treatments when translating; strive for naturalness in the target language while preserving meaning. Expect that certain graces of the original language may be irrecoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colloquialisms and 'cant'—reproduce judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Far be it from me... to value myself upon hitting the words of cant in which my drolling author is so luxuriant; for though such words have stood me in good stead, I scarce can forbear thinking myself unhappy in having insensibly hoarded up so much gibberish and Billingsgate trash in my memory...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colloquial, rough, or vulgar expressions can be useful to preserve the author's character, but the translator should be cautious about boasting of or overusing them; reproduce them where they serve the work, not as mere display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: After all, should this work fail to please the greater number of readers, I am sure it cannot miss being liked by those who are for witty mirth and a chirping bottle; though not by those solid sots who seem to have drudged all their youth long only that they might enjoy the sweet blessing of getting drunk every night in their old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the book’s audience: aim chiefly at readers who appreciate witty mirth and sociable humor. Do not expect the same reception from more sober, solemn readers. Tailor tone and presentation (in translation/preface) to the sensibilities of this audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and address critics and various reader-types
rubrics_metrics.description: If thou art a brother of the quill... If thou art one of those who, though they never write, criticise everyone that does; avaunt!--Thou art a professed enemy of mankind... If thou art one of those critics in dressing... If thou art one of those eavesdroppers, who would have their moroseness be counted gravity, thou wilt condemn a mirth which thou art past relishing;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize typical hostile reactions (envious fellow-writers, amateur critics, morose 'eavesdroppers', dressers-up of learning) and either rebuke, ignore, or preempt them in the preface. Understand that many negative responses stem from personal disposition, not the work’s intrinsic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone toward readerly pity and praise
rubrics_metrics.description: As for wheedling you into a liking of a work, I must confess it seems the safest way; but though flattery pleases you well when it is particular, you hate it, as little concerning you, when it is general... This submission, which sometimes wheedles you into pity, as seldom decoys you into love...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on generic flattery or pleas for pity to win readers. Specific, particularized praise or modest, well-targeted appeals are more effective. Avoid begging for sympathy; it rarely converts pity into genuine appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty about linguistic faults and conciliatory apologies
rubrics_metrics.description: I will not say as much of my writings, in which I study to be as little incorrect as the hurry of business and shortness of time will permit; but I may better say... that what errors may be found in the diction are crept in against my intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When linguistic imperfections occur, acknowledge them briefly and modestly; ask for readers' indulgence while pointing out that many errors are inadvertent. Avoid overlong apologies that draw attention away from the work itself.
